societies.name: The Dancers at the End of Time — Ring-supported humanity
societies.work: The Dancers at the End of Time

scope.continuity: End of Time series setting, before terminal ring failure
scope.period: The continuing ring-supported era before the Lost Cities’ energy depletion
scope.population: Living human and human-derived End of Time residents
exclusions: The final ring failure as unchanged provision
Any magical-looking action as unsupported nontechnical fantasy
Dead or vanished people as leisure beneficiaries

societies.description:
End of Time residents use personal power rings to reshape matter and create their surroundings from ancient stored energy. The supporting Lost Cities make this a technological inheritance rather than an unexplained ability to conjure necessities. Within the functioning system, residents can obtain material conditions through their rings instead of ordinary subsistence employment. Guarantees are rated strong, with the later exhaustion demonstrating a real limit to that apparent abundance.

Practical productive access is widely dispersed among ring users, supporting a distributed human-control estimate. The gathered account does not establish equal control over every part of the ancient energy infrastructure, so the interval remains broad. Appearance, immortality and fantastic scale do not make the users external AI. Their culture is heavily recreational, but constructing experiences, creating art, teaching and caring can all be useful work. Nonworking therefore remains unresolved. The point covers the established supported era rather than the catastrophe or its special time-travel resolution, and does not multiply every time-displaced appearance into a new person.

guarantees.basis: Personal rings alter matter using actual inherited energy infrastructure; their later failure marks a distinct limit rather than absence of earlier support.

control.basis: Widely distributed personal productive access supports human control, while ownership of the underlying Lost Cities remains uncertain.

nonworking.basis: No all-person useful-work census; chosen art, care, research, maintenance and other productive activities still count.

evidence.claim: Personal rings alter matter using actual inherited energy infrastructure; their later failure marks a distinct limit rather than absence of earlier support.
evidence.locator: Bounded named-society economic and story sections

uncertainties: Reference-led provisional assessment; source limitations and editorial uncertainty remain explicit.

societies.name: Mockingbird — Robot-maintained New York
societies.society: The declining human city supported by automatic services

scope.period: Established mechanical support before the protagonists’ later social changes
scope.population: Living human New York residents under the robot service system
exclusions: Decline and death as 100 percent leisure
Spofforth’s copied human memories as unambiguously external AI

societies.description:
Automatic stores dispense food and clothing, while robots maintain the routines on which the remaining population depends. This is actual continuing material support amid institutional decline. Guarantees receive a cautiously favorable estimate because ordinary provision persists, while malfunction, isolation and reproductive damage undermine security. The estimate does not confuse pleasant sedation with the satisfaction of every human need.

Effective control remains unresolved. Robotic administration is clear, but the most important surviving controller, Spofforth, contains edited human memories; the exact relation between that human-derived personality, other machines and inherited rules is not reduced to a simple external-AI coordinate. The AI-provision regime remains provisional. Much ordinary service work is delegated, yet teaching, reading, care and creative activity remain useful human work. No all-person census follows from drug use or a shrinking population, so nonworking stays null. Conflicting exact demographic details in short summaries are excluded, and dead people are never counted as liberated nonworkers.

guarantees.basis: The identified automatic stores and robot maintenance provide ongoing food/clothing/support, with institutional decay and malfunction qualifying its security.

control.basis: Robot administration and Spofforth’s edited human-memory origin leave ultimate human-versus-external-AI control unresolved.

societies.name: 2312 — The spacer necessities economy
societies.society: Cooperative space settlements with quantum-assisted planning

scope.continuity: Kim Stanley Robinson’s 2312 spacer economic model
scope.period: Established space-settlement economy outside the Terminator attack emergency
scope.population: Living human spacer residents of the described cooperative network
exclusions: Every terrarium as autonomous AI sovereign property
The author’s real Mondragon or Antarctica examples as literal fictional locations

societies.description:
The spacer economy supplies necessities on an as-needed, nonmonetary basis while retaining smaller markets for extras. The author explicitly connects this fictional arrangement to shared economic ownership and durable settlement institutions. Quantum computers coordinate the planned economy and its technological habitat network, materially supporting distribution beyond individual wage purchases. Guarantees are strong for the described network, with local differences and frontier conditions left as qualifications.

Control is placed toward shared human ownership because workers and citizens collectively hold the economic system. Computer planning is administration here, not sufficient evidence of autonomous AI sovereignty. The estimate remains broad because the network mixes institutions and the exact powers of planners and local bodies vary. This is not a claim that production requires no people: habitat work, farming, care, transport, research and art remain useful. No all-person participation rate can be derived from free necessities or cooperative organization, so nonworking stays unresolved. Earth’s remaining market economies and specific attack emergencies are outside the scoped baseline.

guarantees.basis: The author explicitly specifies as-needed nonmonetary necessities; quantum-assisted economic coordination and technological habitats support the distribution model.

control.basis: The author describes shared worker/citizen ownership; computer planning is not automatically independent machine sovereignty.

nonworking.basis: No all-person useful-work census; chosen art, care, research, maintenance and other productive activities still count.

evidence.claim: The author explicitly specifies as-needed nonmonetary necessities; quantum-assisted economic coordination and technological habitats support the distribution model.
evidence.locator: Bounded named-society economic and story sections

societies.name: Monk & Robot — Panga’s anti-automation community
societies.work: A Psalm for the Wild-Built / A Prayer for the Crown-Shy
societies.society: The specific back-to-the-land community described during the sequel journey

scope.continuity: Monk & Robot duology; the specific community appears in A Prayer for the Crown-Shy
scope.period: The established community encountered during Dex and Mosscap’s tea-service route
scope.population: Living human members of the explicitly automation-eschewing community
exclusions: The free robot population as forced human workers
General Pangan basics as a verified local transfer charter
Respect for robots as a proven job-protection motive

societies.description:
One Pangan community deliberately rejects automation because it fears a return to the Factory Age. This is a specific technological choice within a wider society that has experienced robot industry and retains access to advanced alternatives. The community is included as an interpretive zero variant based on ecological and social restraint, not as evidence that all Panga protects employment or abandons technology. Human productive activity remains part of its chosen way of life.

The short critical account does not specify local productive ownership, decision procedures or how this community obtains every necessity, so guarantees and control remain unresolved. The broader duology’s accessible basics cannot simply be copied into a precise local entitlement or transfer rule. Robots’ decision to leave industrial service also does not turn them into human-owned automation waiting to be reclaimed. Nonworking remains null because philosophical permission to exist without proving usefulness is not an activity census. The source identifies this community in the sequel; the original discovery title is transparently broadened to the duology rather than claiming the scene occurs in the first novella.

guarantees.basis: The critical review explicitly identifies a community that eschews automation to avoid the Factory Age despite known technological alternatives.

control.basis: The community’s own productive ownership and governance are not specified; a distributed-human analogy remains provisional.

nonworking.basis: No all-person useful-work census; chosen art, care, research, maintenance and other productive activities still count.

evidence.claim: The critical review explicitly identifies a community that eschews automation to avoid the Factory Age despite known technological alternatives.
evidence.locator: Bounded named-society economic and story sections

review_notes: Twelve sequential short checks, four records including one narrowly scoped interpretive zero variant.
The Dancers’ rings draw on actual stored-energy infrastructure; terminal depletion is a different period. Creative production is not presumed nonwork.
Mockingbird has automatic food/clothing but mixed human-memory controller origins; exact conflicting child-demographic claims are not adopted.
2312 explicitly combines non-wage necessities and shared economic ownership with machine-assisted planning; actual human production remains visible.
The Panga zero record is a specific sequel community, not the whole post-robot moon. The first-book discovery title is corrected transparently to the duology.
Emergency Skin’s commons and biotech exclusion do not automatically prove machine production. No obscure novel or full PDF was read to rescue unclear mechanisms.
Harvest of Stars radio broadcasts, Rainbow street addresses, welding specifications and unrelated technical automation papers were discarded.
